Existing pathology platforms offer graphical inspection and analysis. QuPath provides an extensible image-analysis environment (Bankhead et al., 2017). Slideflow Studio supports whole-slide visualisation (Dolezal et al., 2024). WSInfer integrates reusable pretrained models with QuPath (Kaczmarzyk et al., 2024). ZY-Path addresses a focused workflow within this landscape by connecting supported local model loading, distinct analysis modes, spatial inspection and persistent inference records in one desktop application.

QuPath is an open-source digital-pathology application with image visualisation, annotation, quantitative analysis and project-oriented workflows (Bankhead et al., 2017). It already provides a graphical interface and extensibility through scripts and extensions. Scripting is relevant to advanced customisation but is not a prerequisite for every interaction. Its whole-slide and annotation capabilities exceed the current scope of ZY-Path.

Slideflow supports deep-learning development for digital histopathology, with slide processing, model training and real-time whole-slide visualisation (Dolezal et al., 2024). Its official repository explicitly describes Slideflow Studio, model-development functionality, stain-processing tools and visualisation.

No-code deployment removes the need to write inference commands, but it does not remove the need for valid inputs. A .pth suffix cannot identify the network architecture, class order, normalisation or trustworthiness of a file. The interface must expose consequential choices and fail clearly when compatibility is not established. WSInfer's reusable-model approach provides an important precedent for model-aware graphical integration (Kaczmarzyk et al., 2024).

WSInfer makes pretrained deep-learning models reusable in a pathology workflow and integrates inference with QuPath (Kaczmarzyk et al., 2024). Its emphasis on model sharing and a standardised interface is directly relevant to the compatibility and provenance requirements of ZY-Path. It also demonstrates that no-code model use is not a unique invention of this capstone.

Histopathology is a reference method for diagnosing many diseases, including malignancies. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images, the staining of nuclei and cytoplasmic structures provides morphological information that trained professionals interpret in context. Digital imaging makes these observations available for storage, teaching and computational analysis. A model's output, however, is an inference from image appearance and must not be equated with a verified clinical diagnosis (Litjens et al., 2017; Kather et al., 2019). Figure 1.1 is reserved for an authorised H&E example illustrating this tissue context.

citations.paragraph_text: NCT-CRC-HE-100K contains 100,000 colorectal tissue patches across nine categories, while CRC-VAL-HE-7K provides a separate labelled evaluation collection (Kather et al., 2019). This project used the former for training and internal validation and the latter for the recorded 7,180-image test. The actual split manifests and measured results are described in Sections 3.3.2 and 4.2.6.

citations.section: 2.2.1 Digital histopathology and the unit of analysis
citations.paragraph_text: Histopathology examines stained tissue to interpret cellular morphology and tissue architecture. H&E images provide patterns relevant to diagnosis and research, while digital analysis translates those images into computational inputs (Litjens et al., 2017). The unit of analysis must be explicit because an image patch, a larger raster region and a whole-slide pyramid have different sampling and resource requirements.

Cytomine supports collaborative analysis of very large images, image annotation and integration of analysis workflows (Marée et al., 2016). A collaborative web architecture is appropriate where shared images and multi-user annotation are central. It introduces infrastructure and administration considerations that differ from a single-user local desktop application.

Usability inspection and empirical user evaluation answer complementary questions. Inspection can expose inconsistent feedback or inaccessible controls, whereas task observation and questionnaires show how intended users actually experience the system (Yen & Bakken, 2012). Nielsen's heuristics support visible status, user control, consistency, error prevention and recognition rather than recall (Nielsen, 1994).

Task and classification mode are visible before running. Status messages distinguish validation, inference, cancellation and completion, while completed-result metadata remains separate from a pending selection. These decisions apply visibility, consistency, recognition and user control from the usability literature (Nielsen, 1994; Yen & Bakken, 2012); their effect on perceived usability will be assessed through the planned UAT.

The model's softmax output is a normalised score over its classes. It is not automatically calibrated as the probability that an interpretation is correct (Guo et al., 2017). A high-confidence majority class across many tiles can arise from genuine image content, sampling scale, preprocessing mismatch or model/domain limitations. ZY-Path exposes per-tile probabilities and coordinates so these possibilities can be investigated rather than using a coloured map as proof of accuracy. Figure 2.1 distinguishes the three output meanings: whole-image classification, tile-class estimates and pixel segmentation.

Image classification assigns a category to an image or patch, whereas semantic segmentation assigns categories to spatial locations. ZY-Path supports both tasks through separate model pathways. Residual networks use shortcut connections (He et al., 2016), DenseNet uses dense feature reuse (Huang et al., 2017), and EfficientNet applies compound scaling (Tan & Le, 2019).

Architecture selection and application integration answer different questions. Residual networks and EfficientNet provide useful comparative foundations (He et al., 2016; Tan & Le, 2019), while ZY-Path concentrates on reconstructing supported models from metadata and presenting their outputs under explicit contracts. The project evaluates its chosen classifier rather than conducting an architecture benchmark.

Convolutional neural networks support classification and segmentation through learned visual representations. DenseNet provides feature reuse through dense connectivity (Huang et al., 2017). U-Net illustrates an encoder–decoder approach to spatial prediction (Ronneberger et al., 2015), while UPerNet combines multiscale processing for scene parsing (Xiao et al., 2018). Their practical use also depends on apparently small implementation choices: the channel order, numerical range, interpolation method, class order and image scale must agree with the model’s requirements. A visually convincing result does not by itself demonstrate that these choices are correct.

Image classification assigns a category to an image or patch, whereas semantic segmentation assigns categories to spatial locations. ZY-Path supports both tasks through separate model pathways. Residual networks use shortcut connections (He et al., 2016), DenseNet uses dense feature reuse (Huang et al., 2017), and EfficientNet applies compound scaling (Tan & Le, 2019).

DenseNet concatenates earlier feature maps into later layers to encourage feature reuse (Huang et al., 2017). The classifier trained for this project uses four dense blocks with two dense layers each. Its precise configuration, rather than a generic family name, governs checkpoint reconstruction and is reported in Section 3.3.2.

U-Net established an influential encoder–decoder approach to biomedical segmentation with skip connections that preserve spatial information (Ronneberger et al., 2015). UPerNet combines multiscale feature processing for scene parsing (Xiao et al., 2018). The current built-in integration reconstructs UPerNet through Transformers using a Swin Base backbone (Liu et al., 2021). U-Net is relevant background, not the architecture of the built-in segmentation checkpoint.

SUS provides a standard ten-item instrument, but its 0–100 score is not a percentage of tasks completed or a measure of diagnostic accuracy (Brooke, 1996). Interpretation should include sample composition, missing data and the tasks users attempted. Feature-specific ratings and qualitative feedback can explain a SUS result, but should be analysed separately rather than added to the standard SUS calculation.
Source: planned SUS/task analysis rules (Brooke, 1996); results await actual responses.

After completing the tasks, ask participants to rate the following standard SUS statements from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree). Keep their order and wording consistent; analyse these ten items separately from the project-specific questions (Brooke, 1996).

No-code interaction is implemented through explicit task controls and interpretable defaults. The mode, source dimensions and resize backend are visible before execution, and a stored record preserves the settings actually used. Separating model adapters, presentation and persistence also localises responsibility for changes, consistent with modular software design principles (Gamma et al., 1994).

SQLite stores structured records in an embedded, serverless database, making it suitable for a local application without a separately administered database service (Kreibich, 2010; SQLite, n.d.). In ZY-Path it links inference identity and timestamps to task-specific metadata and saved artifacts. Parameterised operations and transactions provide the database component of persistence, while external artifact handling remains the coordinator’s responsibility.

The selected-epoch validation accuracy exceeds external test accuracy by approximately 8.41 percentage points. Internal validation uses a stratified random patch-level split of the same 100,000-image pool as training, without patient grouping. In contrast, the CRC-VAL-HE-7K dataset documentation describes a test cohort of 50 patients with no patient overlap with NCT-CRC-HE-100K (Kather et al., 2018). The two estimates therefore assess different generalisation conditions. Class proportions also differ: ADI represents 10.41% of the 100K pool versus 18.64% of the test set, DEB 11.51% versus 4.72%, and MUS 13.54% versus 8.25%. These results do not isolate the contribution of patient grouping, cohort differences or class composition to the observed gap.

Training used NCT-CRC-HE-100K.zip, the standard Macenko stain-normalised release, rather than the separately distributed NONORM version (Kather et al., 2018). The dataset documentation specifies 224 × 224 pixels at 0.5 μm/pixel for both NCT-CRC-HE-100K and CRC-VAL-HE-7K. Stain normalisation of source images is distinct from raw255 or ImageNet numerical preprocessing of input tensors. Both validation and original test scripts use deterministic Resize, ToTensorV2 and float32 raw255; the Windows application-default Pillow rerun preserves every external-test predicted label. The observed score gap is not evidence of a stain-processing mismatch.

Classification performance is specific to its data and preprocessing. The 90.68% accuracy and 88.59% macro-F1 are reproduced by the original evaluation and the application-default Single image core on native 224 × 224 external-test patches. The dataset documentation identifies the external cohort as patient-independent from NCT-CRC-HE-100K; the internal training/validation split, however, is patch-based and does not enforce patient or slide separation (Kather et al., 2018). Its 99.09% validation accuracy may therefore be optimistic for cross-patient generalisation. The observed gap does not isolate a principal causal factor. Performance on arbitrary resized crops, different physical scales and tiled maps, together with calibration and content-duplicate checks, requires further evaluation.

Source-based UPerNet reconstruction loads its configuration from the local Hugging Face cache with local_files_only=True. The Windows build script and PyInstaller specification now describe how to collect the permitted weights, verified configuration, report font and runtime dependencies (PyInstaller Development Team, n.d.). Frozen execution reads the bundled configuration. These implemented build preparations are distinct from an actual version-matched build and clean-machine offline acceptance, whose status is assessed in Section 4.3.4.

Model trust is a further ethical and technical concern. The loader first attempts supported loading paths, including a weights-only torch.load attempt, but retains a fallback for serialized modules. Such files can execute code during deserialisation. The intended workflow therefore accepts trusted models from known sources; a file-extension filter and dummy forward pass must not be described as a sandbox or malware detector (PyTorch Contributors, n.d.).

Implementation changes replace fixed panel assumptions with draggable splitters, scrollable contents and bounded window restoration. The aim is to keep essential actions reachable while prioritising the analysis image. Figure 3.2 presents an annotated wireframe of this arrangement and its main user actions.

prose_mentions.text: The primary actor is an educational/research user. No administrator or clinical approval role is implemented. Selecting a model includes compatibility validation. Restore saved result and Re-run recorded analysis are separate use cases because only rerun performs inference and creates a new record; Search/filter locates records without executing either operation. MainWindow snapshots the current preferences for ordinary Run or the selected record for Re-run, then starts the worker. Signals deliver progress and a completed result. The coordinator saves completed artifacts and inserts a record only after successful persistence. Figure 3.4 uses guarded alternative fragments for cancellation, pipeline error and persistence failure; these exits are distinct from completed history.
